questions.prompt: A counting semaphore has the value 7. Then 20 P (wait) operations and 15 V (signal) operations complete on it. What is the resulting value of the semaphore?
questions.explanation: Each P decrements and each V increments, so the value is 7 - 20 + 15 = 2. Note that processes blocked along the way do not change the arithmetic, since a blocked P has not completed.

questions.prompt: A shared variable x, initially 0, is used by four concurrent processes. W and X each read x, add one, and store it. Y and Z each read x, subtract two, and store it. Every process performs P(S) before reading and V(S) after storing, where S is a counting semaphore initialised to 2. What is the maximum possible final value of x?
questions.explanation: S = 2 admits two processes at once, so updates can be lost. Let W read 0 and stall; then Y and Z run fully, leaving x = -4; now W stores 0 + 1 = 1, and finally X reads 1 and stores 2. Both decrements are overwritten, giving the maximum of 2.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is NOT one of the three requirements a solution to the critical section problem must satisfy?

options.text: Bounded waiting
Deadlock detection
Progress
Mutual exclusion

questions.explanation: The three classical requirements are mutual exclusion, progress and bounded waiting. Deadlock detection is a resource-allocation concern, not a property demanded of a critical-section protocol.

questions.prompt: Semaphores can be used to solve which of the following?

options.text: Deadlock detection only
Mutual exclusion only
Page replacement and mutual exclusion
Race conditions, process synchronisation and mutual exclusion

questions.explanation: A binary semaphore enforces mutual exclusion and thereby removes race conditions, while a counting semaphore can sequence events between processes. Page replacement is unrelated to semaphores.

questions.prompt: A busy-wait lock is built with an atomic test-and-set instruction. Which statement about it is correct?

options.text: It guarantees mutual exclusion and is deadlock free, but not starvation free
It requires processes to enter the critical section in FIFO order
It allows two processes into the critical section simultaneously
It guarantees both mutual exclusion and bounded waiting

questions.explanation: Test-and-set is atomic, so mutual exclusion holds and some waiting process always succeeds. But nothing orders the waiters, so one unlucky process can be overtaken indefinitely — bounded waiting fails.

questions.prompt: In the producer-consumer problem with a bounded buffer, increasing the number of buffer slots is likely to:

options.text: Guarantee the consumer never waits
Eliminate the possibility of deadlock entirely
Increase throughput by reducing how often either party blocks
Remove the need for mutual exclusion on the buffer

questions.explanation: More slots absorb bursts, so the producer fills up and the consumer empties out less often. Mutual exclusion on the shared buffer is still required, and a badly ordered wait can still deadlock.

questions.prompt: Processes X, Y and Z each need semaphores from the set {a, b, c, d}, all binary and initialised to 1. Which ordering of P operations is guaranteed to be deadlock free?

options.text: X: a,b,c   Y: b,c,d   Z: a,c,d
X: a,b,c   Y: b,c,d   Z: c,d,a
X: b,a,c   Y: c,b,d   Z: a,d,c
X: a,c,b   Y: d,b,c   Z: c,a,d

questions.explanation: In the correct ordering every process acquires semaphores in the same global order a < b < c < d, which makes a circular wait impossible. The other orderings each contain a process that grabs a later semaphore before an earlier one.

questions.prompt: Why must semaphore P and V operations be executed atomically?

options.text: Because they always require a system call
Because the scheduler cannot preempt kernel code
Otherwise two processes could both observe the semaphore as available and enter together
Otherwise the semaphore value would overflow

questions.explanation: The test and the decrement must be indivisible. If a process is preempted between reading a positive value and decrementing it, another can read the same value, and both proceed into the critical section.

questions.prompt: A solution to the dining philosophers problem that avoids deadlock is:

options.text: Each philosopher waits a random time before picking up either fork
Every philosopher picks up the right fork first, then the left
One philosopher picks up the right fork first while all others pick up the left first
Every philosopher picks up the left fork first, then the right

questions.explanation: Making one philosopher asymmetric breaks the circular wait, so at least one can always eat. Uniform ordering deadlocks when all five pick up simultaneously, and random delays only make deadlock less likely, not impossible.

questions.prompt: Which sharing property must a program have so that a single copy in memory can serve several users concurrently?

options.text: It must be recursive
It must be reentrant
It must be compiled without optimisation
It must be written as a macro

questions.explanation: A reentrant program keeps no modifiable state in its code segment, holding per-user data in registers or a private stack. Editors and compilers are shared this way. Recursion is a different and unrelated property.
